slides.title: Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A kidney biopsy is a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination. It can supply two kinds of evidence. Histology is the microscopic examination of tissue. It reveals injury and inflammation that can support a rejection diagnosis.

Molecular measurements count selected types of RNA, which include messages cells make when genes are active. Those measurements reflect both gene activity within cells and the mix of cells in the tissue. More immune cells in a specimen can also change its RNA pattern.

The tissue's appearance and its RNA pattern describe different aspects of the biopsy. Molecular tests already have a recognized role in parts of rejection assessment. That established application provides the context for this project.

slides.title: Purpose of this project
paragraphs: Molecular measurements already have a recognized role in parts of transplant rejection assessment. I used this established application to investigate a practical modeling choice: how much does the classifier change the rejection cases missed and the false flags produced?
The purpose was to assess what a more complex model contributes before pursuing further validation, and to build scoring software that preserves the evaluated procedure.

The main comparison is CatBoost against regularized multigene logistic regression. I compare them on the same specimens, using the diagnoses recorded in the public dataset as the reference. That lets me examine both the size of an observed difference and how much confidence to place in it.
The next slide shows where this application is already recognized and why both kinds of error matter.
actions: Explain why the comparison is useful within an established application. Connect the modeling decision to the software that preserves it.

slides.title: Clinical and research context
paragraphs: Banff is a framework specialists use to classify transplant biopsy findings. Its current guidance includes thoroughly validated biopsy transcript tests in defined settings for antibody-mediated rejection. That gives molecular assessment an established clinical context. It does not confer that validation on my classifier.

Zhang and colleagues provide the public B-HOT data. Their four-class study already compared regularized regression with other approaches, including gradient boosting. They selected LASSO, a form of regularized regression, because accuracy was similar and it can use fewer weighted features. Their result is a reason to take the simpler comparator seriously.

My contribution is an independent binary comparison of any recorded rejection versus no rejection, with explicit preprocessing, error counts and reproducible scoring software. It does not reproduce their four-class model.

Both errors matter in this application. Missed rejection can leave kidney injury untreated. A false rejection diagnosis can lead to medicines that suppress the immune system and worsen an infection. This project measures classifier errors against recorded diagnoses. Added clinical value from this particular score would need direct evaluation.
actions: Explain Banff briefly, then the source study and its reason for choosing LASSO. Connect both errors to the established application.

slides.title: What the dataset contains
paragraphs: The public data come in two downloads: a metadata file and an archive containing 1,395 individual count files. I assembled them into the two tables shown here.

The count table has one row per biopsy specimen and a column for each of the 770 RNA counts. The specimen-information table contains the recorded diagnosis and the study group assigned by the authors.
Specimen ID is unique in each table and matches the rows one to one. GSM6510425 is the same specimen in both. This pairs the measurements with the diagnosis used for training and evaluation.

The 1,395 specimens include 1,193 transplant biopsies and 202 native-kidney controls. I included all of them in my comparison. The article reports those control counts, but the public specimen metadata do not identify which no-rejection rows are native kidneys.

The full study does not document separation by patient or referring center between study groups. It reports referrals from several regions, but all specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories. Geographic breadth does not establish separation by patient or referring center.

slides.title: Outcome: rejection versus no rejection
paragraphs: The public dataset records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.

Those three diagnoses all count as rejection. The fourth category, no rejection, includes normal tissue and other kidney diseases. The authors excluded some diagnostic categories rather than assigning them to no rejection. I trained the models to predict these recorded labels.
I also retained the original diagnoses. That let me examine whether the missed cases were concentrated in a particular kind of rejection.

slides.title: The measurements used to build the features
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 counts of selected RNA types. The 758 model measurements include human and viral RNA. Their signals reflect both gene activity and the mixture of cells in the biopsy. Their normalized values become the model's inputs.
The other 12 measure relatively stable housekeeping RNAs. More usable RNA entering the assay can raise counts across many measurements. The reference helps adjust for that overall difference.
I used the housekeeping counts for normalization, then excluded them from the model. The next slide shows the calculation.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: For each of the 758 counts, I used the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in my public example, starting with its raw count of four.
Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.
Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.
actions: Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.

2. Calculate log2(count + 1): 2.322
3. Average log2(count + 1) for the 12 reference RNAs: 7.900
4. Subtract that reference: 2.322 − 7.900 = −5.578

slides.title: Models compared
paragraphs: Each model produces a rejection score. I call it a score because calibration has not established reliable individual probabilities here.
The constant model uses the training rejection fraction for everyone. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.

IFNG encodes interferon gamma, an immune-signalling protein associated with T-cell-mediated rejection. I used logistic regression with this one normalized measurement as a simple benchmark. It was fixed in the starting recipe, rather than selected as the best individual predictor.
The all-RNA model also used logistic regression, but combined all 758 normalized measurements using learned weights. Regularization limited those weights to reduce overfitting.

CatBoost can capture nonlinear patterns and interactions. One RNA measurement's relationship with rejection can depend on another measurement's level. It works with numerical inputs, so categorical features are not required. Shallow trees and a small learning rate help limit overfitting.

The comparison uses the same specimens and normalization. The main comparison is all-RNA logistic regression versus CatBoost, with IFNG and the constant model as supporting benchmarks. I examine how their missed rejection and false positives differ.

slides.title: Selecting the model and threshold
paragraphs: A threshold turns a score into a rejection flag. Recall starts with all cases diagnosed as rejection and counts how many the model flags correctly. Precision starts with all rejection flags and counts how many agree with a recorded rejection diagnosis.
I chose a screening target of at least 90 percent recall, then minimized false positives. ROC-AUC broke ties. This was an experiment choice, not a clinical requirement.

Both models detected 157 of 174 screening rejection cases. CatBoost made five false positives among 89 no-rejection specimens. Logistic regression made six. That one-case difference selected CatBoost under the rule.

I kept the selected model and threshold fixed for evaluation. Screening explains the original selection. The separate validation results show how the models compared afterward. Choosing a threshold does not calibrate the score.
actions: Explain each denominator, then the screening rule and the five-versus-six result. Keep the original selection distinct from the later validation comparison.
visible_cues: Recall = correctly flagged rejection cases / all cases diagnosed as rejection. False negatives are missed cases.
Precision = correctly flagged rejection cases / all rejection flags. False positives are incorrect flags.
Screening rule: detect at least 90% of recorded rejection cases, then minimize false positives. ROC-AUC breaks ties.

slides.title: Validation results
paragraphs: Here are the results on the same 345 validation specimens. False negatives are missed cases among 169 specimens recorded as rejection. False positives are incorrect flags among 176 recorded as no rejection.

The IFNG-only model has 14 false negatives and 75 false positives. All-RNA logistic regression has 33 false negatives and eight false positives. CatBoost has 25 false negatives and also eight false positives.

CatBoost therefore missed eight fewer rejection cases than logistic regression, with the same false-positive count. That validation result adds evidence in its favor beyond the narrow screening result. However, the paired uncertainty interval for the recall difference includes zero.

I also completed a discovery-only follow-up with 20 different splits, each separating fitting, selection and assessment. CatBoost was selected 13 times and logistic regression seven. The repetitions overlap, and the choice varied with the split. Taken together, the results leave a dependable preference between the models unsettled.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false positives but 11 more false negatives. Its validation recall is 85.2 percent, below the 90 percent screening target. Which tradeoff is preferable would depend on how specialists use the result.
The constant model flags everyone at its fixed threshold of 0.5. It misses none of the 169 rejection cases but falsely flags all 176 no-rejection cases.

slides.title: Shared preparation and scoring
paragraphs: The main software decision was to keep one preparation calculation for the analysis and the application. A difference between them could change the score even when the raw measurements are identical.

This excerpt is the prediction entry point for raw counts. The first line calls normalize_counts, the same function used during model development. It checks the measurements and applies the housekeeping adjustment. The schema supplies the required measurement names and their expected order.
The second line passes those normalized values to the saved model. The prediction code then compares the score with its saved threshold and attaches the model version.

Both the command-line tool and the web application call this prediction code. If I later change an input check, I can make that change in one place and check both routes. The short method makes that shared calculation easy to find and review.

slides.title: An interface other software can call
paragraphs: The web page is one way to use the model. I also gave it an API: a documented way for another program to send measurements and receive results. A developer could connect their own application to this interface.

The request sends a CSV containing a specimen ID and the 770 raw counts, including the 12 housekeeping measurements. The ID keeps each result attached to the right source record. It does not enter the model.

The response is structured JSON that another program can read. This example shows the same specimen from the demo, with its score, threshold, and flag. The model version and input-schema version accompany each result. They identify the saved model and the expected set of measurements.
Keeping those fields together lets another application explain the decision and record how I calculated it. The service uses its configured model and threshold for every request.

slides.title: Checking the application against the analysis
paragraphs: Moving a model into an application should preserve its answers. I checked that by sending all 345 validation specimens through a running HTTP service, then comparing its results with the command-line tool and the saved analysis.

I deliberately reversed the input columns. A valid file should produce the same answer when its columns change position, because the software matches measurements by name. The verification code also checks the specimen IDs before comparing their results.

The assertion on this slide compares the HTTP scores with the command-line scores. I allowed an absolute difference of one times ten to the minus twelve for numerical rounding. The same script also compares the saved analysis scores and checks the rejection flags. All 345 results agreed within the tolerance, and every flag matched.
The table shows two failures I tested. Missing or duplicate measurements stop the whole batch, with no partial predictions. Incompatible model metadata stops the model from loading.

These checks test whether the application performs the intended calculation and handles the tested failures. The separate model evaluation answers how often that calculation agrees with the recorded diagnosis.

slides.title: Running and maintaining the application
paragraphs: For another developer to use this work, the setup needs to be explicit. The repository includes a locked dependency list, commands to install the application, and instructions to reproduce the analysis or run the saved model.

I added automated checks that run when code is pushed or a pull request is opened. They check the installed package, run the tests, and build a container with a small synthetic model. This keeps routine checks independent of the public dataset and the full training run.

The verification record includes a successful hosted run for an earlier revision. The later application changes have separate local checks. I also built and tested a local container with the actual research model, including valid predictions and an invalid request.
That gives a developer documented setup, repeatable checks, and a tested way to run the application. The cloud deployment remains future work.

slides.title: What this project accomplished
paragraphs: Within an established molecular application, this comparison shows what CatBoost contributed: eight fewer missed validation rejection cases than logistic regression, with eight false positives each. A dependable advantage remains uncertain.
I also built software that preserves the calculation, with a versioned score, clear input errors and checks against saved results.
Cross-validation within discovery is the next modeling step. Whether adding this particular score improves clinical assessment still needs direct evaluation.
Zhang and colleagues supplied the public data. AI assisted with development and this presentation. Thank you.
